newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FOCUS-China curbs take hot money out of HK stocks.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-China curbs take hot money out of HK stocks.

text.p: China's recent drive to curb speculation in its booming stock markets has siphoned hot money out of Hong Kong's red chips, but China-plays should continue to be a favoured investment theme, analysts said on Friday.
"We are still positive on red chips but buying should be more selective," said Yamaichi International analyst Ben Tam.
Beijing ordered state banks last week to stop trading in stocks and wind up their positions within 10 days.
"Mainland companies in Hong Kong also need to repatriate money to China if they borrowed from banks to speculate on Hong Kong shares," said Josephine Hui, head of research at Cheerful Research.
Red chips stocks -- or Hong Kong-incorporated companies with financial backing from the mainland -- have been the main target of this money in Hong Kong, analysts said.

Although it was hard to quantify the amounts involved, analysts said the flow of money was responsible for a rush for China plays from the fourth quarter of last year, boosting overall sentiment in the territory's market.

"If all the Chinese money was sent back to China the whole market would cool down," said Tam. "During the heaviest trading days over the past weeks, volume on red chips accounted for more than 50 percent of total turnover."
Total turnover for May was HK$344 billion ($44.4 billion) , up 71 percent from HK$200 billion in April, the Hong Kong stock exchange said.

Red chips have been the most speculative sector of the market and were hardest hit by a correction this week. "They fell about eight percent on Thursday alone before regaining some ground on Friday," one broker said.
Deutsche Morgan Grenfell analyst Andrew Keut said the slump had knocked about five points off the 1997 price earnings ratio of red chips to 25 times from 30 times.
Some analysts said a shake-out on Thursday, which saw the blue chip Hang Seng Index tumble 497.18 points, coincided with Beijing's deadline for repatriating funds.
The Hang Seng recovered 188.21 points to close at 14,112.55 on Friday after hitting a day low of 13,795 in morning trade.
"Market sentiment has improved with mainland investors buying red-chips," said Michael Ng, dealing director at Sassoon Securities.

Analysts said investors had also snapped up red chip shares ahead of the launch on Monday of a new Hang Seng China-Affiliated Corporations Index which includes some of Hong Kong's favourite China-play shares.
The 32-company index will track the performance of locally-listed companies with signficant equity interest held by entities in China.

Analysts said this week's heavy sell off would mean further mainland selling was likely to be limited. The fundamentals of red chip companies also remained the same and investors would continue to seek exposure to China, they said.
